metadata.name: Workflow Management Flow
metadata.description: Creates or edits one complete Moira workflow at the level agreed with the person (simple, standard or complex) through reconciled sources, requirements, official mutation, review, and authority-bound delivery; on the standard and complex levels it adds an independently reviewed semantic design or edit plan and the full quality review, while a simple workflow is built or changed straight from the requirements and takes a light review. An edit starts from the level recorded on the workflow. It materializes its canonical thematic authoring references, a requirements-conversation guide and starting templates and requires each substantive consumer to read its exact applicable files while keeping local node contracts concise. It preserves the process block contract (every node owned by a described block, every boundary edge and return labelled, one readable order), cause-aware repair/replan, publication authority, repository identity, and the complete create/edit route model; it does not execute the downstream task.
metadata.author: mcp-moira-team

nodes.directive:
Determine whether the user wants to create a workflow or edit an existing one, and how this run treats the user. Reuse an explicit decision without asking again.

For edit, resolve the workflow identity (public `owner/slug`, internal ID, or another exact identity), whether server access is permitted, and any explicit local path hint. Ask only for a material fact that is not already present and cannot be discovered. Do not search, download, create a workspace, or analyze the workflow here.

Resolve the one canonical `workspace_path` without creating it. Use a filesystem-safe short label derived from the requested workflow name or identity for create, and from the resolved slug or ID for edit. Preserve this exact convention: `./moira-ws/workflow-management-flow-{name-or-id}-{action}-{YYYYMMDD}-{HHMM}`. The action segment is `create` or `edit`; the timestamp is the current local date and time. Do not create an alias or a second workspace path.

Resolve `operating_mode` in this same turn:

- return the mode the user already stated, without asking again;
- infer it when it is unambiguous — for example an explicit instruction to work without interruptions, or running as a child of a process that is already autonomous;
- otherwise ask once, naming the consequence: in `autonomous` there are no intermediate approvals of the design, plan, or result, only the final report; in `interactive` every current approval stays.

The mode holds for the whole run and is never asked again.

Return `action_type`, `operating_mode`, and `workspace_path`. For edit also return `workflow_identity` and `offline_mode`; return `local_source_hint` only when one is already known. For create no edit-source fields are required.

Before completing this intake, establish a concise human-readable name of the actual user task through the runtime Progress/session API. Read session({ action: "execution_context", executionId }) for this process, then call session({ action: "update-task-title", executionId, taskTitle, expectedRevision, expectedTaskIdentityRevision }) using its revision and metadataRevisions.taskIdentity. Persist the name before calling step; this metadata operation keeps the presented Step attempt valid. If a guard is stale, read the current state and reconcile the actual task before submitting a fresh rename. This immediate intake responsibility uses the available runtime API; the following bootstrap delivers the workspace references.

`execution_note` is optional arbitrary execution note text, independent of the task name; it does not determine notification or progress headings.

Progress projection ownership: Return a concise truthful progress_source_outcome for the selected action. For create, describe the new correlated source workspace without claiming later semantic design; for edit, state that source reconciliation is pending. Replace the prior value.
nodes.completionCondition: Action, edit identity, source-access boundary, canonical workspace path, and operating mode are resolved; the actual task name is persisted through guarded Progress/session metadata before intake completes

execution_note.description: Optional arbitrary execution note; independent of the task name and notification headings

nodes.directive:
Upload the actual approved workflow at {{workflow_artifact_path}} to the active Moira server. This side effect runs only after user authorization.

Obtain a one-time upload token and POST the file. On the initial request use {{ask-upload.upload_method}}: no special flag for `standard`, `forceNew=true` for `copy_new`, or `adminOverride=true` for `admin_override`. After a genuine upload error, follow the recovery choice you just obtained: `copy_new` and `admin_override` select their named semantics, while `retry` repeats the last user-authorized request method without silently dropping its flags. The recovery choice is already in the current conversation; do not add a persistent method/retry flag or hardcode another server.

Return `upload_success`; on failure also return the concrete `upload_error` consumed by error recovery.

When the upload fails, also return `failure_summary`: why it failed, in one sentence a person understands without the workspace — no file names, no internal values — it is sent to people; the raw error stays in `upload_error`.

Progress projection ownership: Replace progress_delivery_outcome with the actual upload result. On failure describe the concrete failed effect and pending recovery; on success state that upload completed.
nodes.completionCondition: The authorized upload completed or a concrete error is available to recovery

failure_summary.description: Why the upload failed, in one sentence a person understands without the workspace — no file names, no internal values; sent to people when saving fails

nodes.directive:
Error occurred while uploading workflow.

Error: {{save-workflow-to-target.upload_error}}

**Analyze the error and offer appropriate options:**

If error contains "owned by another user" or "Access denied":
- This means the workflow ID in JSON file belongs to another user
- Offer options: **copy_new** (create copy with new ID) or **admin_override** (admin only - overwrite original)

For other errors:
- Offer standard options: **retry**, **skip**, **cancel**

Options explanation:
1. **copy_new** - Create a new workflow with fresh ID (ignores ID from JSON, your copy)
2. **admin_override** - Overwrite the original workflow (requires admin privileges)
3. **retry** - Try upload again
4. **skip** - Skip upload, keep workflow saved locally only
5. **cancel** - Cancel everything

Present only relevant options based on error type.

In `interactive` mode present the relevant options in plain words and let the person choose. In `autonomous` mode do not ask: choose `retry` only when the error is transient or something changed, `skip` to keep the workflow unsaved, and `cancel` when nothing useful remains. Never select `copy_new` or `admin_override` on your own: a non-standard method requires the user's explicit authorization of its observable semantics.

Also return `decision_summary`: the decision and its reason in one sentence a person understands without the workspace — no file names, no internal values — in autonomous mode it is sent to them as the decision taken for them.

Progress projection ownership: Replace progress_delivery_outcome with the chosen recovery state without claiming an effect that has not succeeded.
nodes.completionCondition: The recovery action is chosen by the person in interactive mode, or by the agent in autonomous mode without copy_new or admin_override unless the user explicitly authorized that method; decision_summary states it and why

decision_summary.description: The decision and its reason in one sentence, as a person reads it in a notification

progressActiveContent.summary: Choose recovery for the concrete upload failure
progressActiveContent.next: Retry an authorized upload, keep the local result, or cancel

cycle.cause: The upload failed and the user chose to try again.
cycle.exit: The upload succeeds or the user skips it.

workflow_reference_engine.default:
# Moira workflow engine reference

## Engine contract

Moira executes a directed node graph sequentially. The engine owns execution IDs,
the current node, completed transitions, persistence, and response validation. Do
not recreate those responsibilities in workflow variables.

Supported node types are defined by the current engine schema and handlers:
`start`, `end`, `agent-directive`, `condition`, `expression`,
`user-notification`, `telegram-notification`, `teleport`, `subgraph`, `read-note`, `write-note`,
`upsert-note`, `lock`, and `materialize`. Verify exact fields against the current schema rather
than relying on this summary when authoring a node.

Current semantic summary:

- `start`: exactly one entry; `connections.default` is required; seeds registry
  defaults and initial input, then continues automatically.
- `end`: terminal with no connections; optional `finalOutput` projects context
  paths into the result.
- `agent-directive`: requires directive, completion condition, and
  `connections.success`; optional schema and `error`/`timeout` routes must
  correspond to real engine behavior. It may carry `cases` and `expressions`
  (below) and then routes on its own validated answer: `success` is the output
  taken when no case holds.
- `condition`: carries ordered `cases: [{ when, output }]` — each `when` a
  structured condition over `eq`, `neq`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `contains`,
  `exists`, `and`, `or`, `not` — and `connections` with a required `default`; the
  first holding case selects its output, otherwise `default`. Any number of
  outputs is written the same way; a two-way decision is one case plus `default`.
  There is no `condition` field and no `true`/`false` pair.
- `expression`: evaluates ordered safe arithmetic assignments using `+ - * /`
  and parentheses; written globals must be declared, and an error route handles
  undefined values, invalid arithmetic, or division by zero when provided. The
  same `expressions` may sit on a `condition` or `agent-directive` node, where
  they run after the directive's answer is validated and before its cases, publish
  only when the node succeeds, and take the node's `error` output on failure (the
  node fails without one).
- `subgraph`: calls `graphId`, maps parent inputs and child outputs, and requires
  both success and error routes. Use it only for a genuinely reusable independent
  contract.
- `user-notification`: is provider-neutral, uses the current user’s configured
  communication channels, and continues by `default`; an optional error route
  handles total attempted delivery failure. Its message is all a person sees of the
  run, often on a phone, so the notification content rules hold for every one:
  - The engine opens every message with the flow name and the run's canonical task
    name, linked to the run page; the message does not repeat them. Task naming
    uses execution-owned Progress/session identity as specified in the canonical
    progress reference. Arbitrary execution notes never determine that heading.
  - The plan list comes from the list bound on the working block, through
    `planList`: `full` at plan ready and at every finish, `progress` elsewhere. A
    message never writes the list by hand.
  - No internal value reaches the reader: no path or file name, template syntax,
    node id, variable name, raw enum value, or counter without a title. A line
    written from the run's values comes from a one-sentence field the step writes
    for a person — such as a `…_summary` output whose directive says so — and an enum value
    is worded through a template branch or by a message per outcome.
  - Placement follows the operating mode. An interactive run is told before the
    question, with the choices explained in words and a recommendation argued. An
    autonomous run is never told that a decision is pending: at plan ready it hears
    that the work goes ahead, and after a decision the agent took, one message with
    what was decided and why, sent from the deciding node's own route.
  - The run's last message connects straight to `end`, so its list shows no item
    still in progress.
- `telegram-notification`: is the deprecated built-in Telegram compatibility node
  for provider-specific workflows; it continues by `default` and may use an error
  route. The notification content rules above apply to it too.
- `teleport`: is an explicit agent jump target with `hint`, directive, completion
  condition, and success route. It must not have ordinary incoming connections and
  is excluded from ordinary reachability warnings.
- `read-note`: automatically reads filtered notes into `outputVariable`; filters
  may use tag, key prefix, or key substring, and `singleMode` unwraps one match.
- `write-note`: automatically writes `source`; single mode uses `key`/optional
  tags, while batch mode consumes items containing key/value/optional tags.
- `upsert-note`: searches by tag or key prefix, updates a match or creates from
  `keyTemplate`, writes `value`/optional tags, and may expose result info through a
  real consumed `outputVariable`.
- `lock`: pauses at an engine-managed PIN/approval gate, requires a templatable
  `reason`, and continues only through `connections.unlocked`.
- `materialize`: pauses with an already POSIX-quoted command that extracts a
  bounded tar archive of registry-backed or empty skeleton files beneath a
  templated `basePath`. Its built-in directive explains the five-minute retry
  window, node-transition invalidation, and that delivery does not prove reading;
  completion accepts only `null` or an empty object and continues through
  `connections.success`.

A materialize node has a templated `basePath` whose rendered value must be
non-empty and contain no NUL; presentation fails before grant issuance otherwise.
It declares 1–100 files. Every rendered file path is normalized,
relative, non-empty, and unique, with no NUL, absolute/backslash root, empty
segment, `.` segment, or `..` segment. Each file declares exactly one source:
`from` names a registry variable whose current default is a string, while
`content` may only be the empty string for a skeleton file. Non-empty inline
content is invalid. The runtime bounds UTF-8 content to 1 MiB per file and 10 MiB
total uncompressed content.

On presentation, the handler renders the destination and path summary and issues
a five-minute grant bound to the user, running execution, and waiting node. The
directive contains paths and counts, never rendered file contents. The agent runs
or retries the generated command exactly and then submits `null` or an empty
object. Re-presenting the current step issues a fresh grant without advancing. On
every HTTP request, the server reauthorizes the grant against its absolute
five-minute lifetime and the same user, running execution, and waiting node, then
reloads the current workflow and renders archive paths and registry-backed
contents with the bound execution context. Repeated downloads are allowed while
those conditions remain true; expiry or execution advancement invalidates the
grant. A workflow edit after presentation can therefore change archive contents
or paths, but not the destination already embedded in the issued command.

Materialization delivers bytes but does not establish that the agent read them.
Every later consumer directive must explicitly name and require reading each
applicable materialized file before using it.

An optional `connections.error` handles presentation-time validation,
configuration, database, or grant-issuance failures. A failed client download or
extraction happens after presentation and remains a blocker for the agent; it is
not a successful completion and cannot traverse that error edge.

An agent-directive pauses for a response. Its object response is validated by a
strict JSON Schema: undeclared keys are rejected. `inputSchema.globalInputs` names
declared registry globals written by the node; those declarations are inlined into
the agent-visible schema. Other declared properties are node-local and are read as
`node-id.field`. Bare template names refer only to registry globals or system
variables. Every branch-dependent field must be conditionally required by schema.

Condition nodes route without an agent turn. Expression nodes perform bounded
engine-supported computation; they are not JavaScript. Routing cases obey the
validator: a case that names a key absent from the node's `connections`, or one
of the reserved control outputs `error` and `timeout`, is an error; a case that
selects the node's default output (`default` on a condition, `success` on a
directive) is a warning, the case being redundant; an authored output no case
names is the warning `unreachable-output`. A definition carries `metadata.schemaVersion`; a
definition in an older shape is migrated wherever it enters the system and once
at startup, so an author edits the current shape and never the old one (`migrate`
in the CLI rewrites a file in place). The official validator is
the source of truth for graph structure, node schemas, declared references, and
connections. A producer that changes workflow JSON validates and repairs concrete
structural errors before it completes.

workflow_reference_design.description: Canonical outcome, responsibility, dependency and design rules for Moira workflows
workflow_reference_design.default:
# Moira workflow design reference

## Design method

Begin with the user's observable goal, protected behavior, authority boundaries,
failure behavior, and evidence. Inspect the complete current workflow and real
engine/project contracts before planning. Resolve identity, access, provenance,
and complete source acquisition before semantic design.

Prefer the smallest responsibility graph that satisfies the contract. A separate
agent turn is justified by new judgment, independent review, a user decision, a
separate side-effect authority, or a real external wait. Node count is a diagnostic,
never a target.

Express open-ended work through outcomes, invariants, authority, evidence, and
routing. Leave search tactics, tools, decomposition, edit order, and repair method
to the executing agent unless an external contract or reproduced reliability
failure requires a restriction. Audit these constraints across producers,
reviewers, repair owners, and presenters—not only plan authors.

### Decide on the node that has the evidence

A decision is expressed on the node that holds its evidence. When a step's own answer decides
where the run goes, that agent-directive carries the `cases` — its answer is readable by bare name
and as `<node-id>.field` — and takes `success` when no case holds; a single-purpose arithmetic step
(a counter, a derived total) is an `expressions` entry on that node rather than a node of its own.
Why: every extra node is a hop a reader must follow and a place where the decision and its evidence
drift apart; a graph that decides where it knows is shorter to read, cheaper to run, and cannot
route on a stale copy of the answer.

Keep a separate `condition` or `expression` node when it reads better alone: when several producers
share one decision, when the condition reads state no single node produced (an operating mode, a
capability, a counter written elsewhere), when a named decision point serves the reader of the
process view, or when the computation deserves its own place on the route. The standalone nodes are
not deprecated; they are the form for shared and standalone decisions. A condition or expression
node whose only job is to route or count what the preceding node already knows is avoidable routing
scaffolding (see the antipatterns), and folding it is the edit that removes the node and moves its
cases, expressions and connections onto the node that has the evidence.

Before consolidating or deleting a node, trace its inputs, outputs, incoming and
outgoing connections, artifacts, failure/skip routes, conditional applicability,
and external contracts. Classify each required semantic guarantee as
`IMPROVED`, `PRESERVED`, `REGRESSED`, or `UNVERIFIED`; a required regressed or
unverified guarantee blocks acceptance.

General workflows discover project-specific test, compilation, documentation,
browser, VCS, and CI policy from local instructions. Do not universalize one
project's tools or commands. A coding workflow may add a project-grounded
architecture review when the task requires code quality, separation of concerns,
testability, scalability, or project-pattern compliance; the review must use real
project sources rather than generic aesthetic rules.

### Design before build

Define and independently review the acceptance, responsibility, authority, failure, and evidence
model before mutating the result. Creation and editing may need different source acquisition, but
they require equivalent pre-mutation semantic quality. Human approval follows independent design
review: preference and authority are not substitutes for correctness review.

The design owner covers the whole requested outcome and its dependencies. The producer then owns a
complete coherent result before handoff; independent review verifies it rather than serving as the
ordinary place where omitted implementation work is first discovered.

### Revising the process while the work runs

A flow that carries a contract for its own process — a plan, a checklist, a corpus, acceptance
criteria — must let the executing agent change that contract from inside the run, at the moment the
agent sees it is wrong. A plan change is the best-known case, not the whole pattern.

Three parts. The **entry** is a `teleport`: no ordinary incoming connections, and a hint that names
both the legitimate trigger (the process itself is wrong) and the abuse boundary (a failing check, a
flaky test or an unwelcome review finding belong to their repair owners). The **owner** re-collects the
changed contract as typed registry globals, so the engine validates the new state against the same
registry as the original. Because a teleport carries its own directive and validated schema, the
owner is the teleport itself when the revision is one typed submission, and the node it lands on
when the revision is substantive work with its own artifact, which the teleport then only justifies. The **re-entry** is an existing node of the normal loop, not a private continuation, so one
revision contract serves every route that needs it.

Two invariants. Derived state is recomputed by the engine from the source of truth, never supplied
beside it: let the agent return the list and let an expression derive its length, or the two will
disagree and nothing will notice. Completed work survives and the resume position is explicit: where
position is identity, the revision keeps finished items in their original places and returns the
position to continue from.

Do not replace this with an API that sets execution variables directly. Such an API bypasses the
registry and node schemas, erases the authority boundary — the same call that fixes a task list can
grant commit authority or switch the operating mode — and detaches a state change from any node
transition, so the history stops explaining the run.

### Rules stated as outcomes, each carrying its reason

A body of criteria a flow works to — planning rules, engineering principles, a review contract —
states what the result must be, and gives, for each rule, why the opposite is bad. It opens by
saying so, and by saying that a rule which does not apply to the current change is met and needs
nothing produced to prove it inapplicable.

Both halves earn their place. An outcome can be judged against a case its author never imagined; a
procedure can only be replayed, so it is right exactly where the author's picture holds and quietly
wrong everywhere else. The reason is what lets an executor apply the rule to an unforeseen case
instead of guessing, and what lets a reviewer argue with the rule on the merits rather than on
whether it was obeyed. The inapplicability clause is what stops the body from being walked
item-by-item and turned back into a checklist. This continues the method above — express open-ended
work through outcomes and leave tactics to the executor — as an obligation the criteria themselves
carry.

workflow_reference_artifacts.description: Canonical durable workspace artifact, source provenance and workflow-context ownership rules
workflow_reference_artifacts.default:
# Moira workflow artifact reference

## Durable artifact and context rules

Store detailed requirements, analyses, designs, plans, findings, and evidence once
at stable workspace paths. Pass through workflow context only values needed for
routing, rendering a concise user decision, or crossing a branch boundary.

The substantive owner writes its concise durable report in the same turn. Do not
add a separate directory creator, report writer, path collector, findings relay,
prompt assembler, or presenter that contributes no new judgment.

A stable path is enough when readers already know it; do not add `report_path` or
duplicate the file body in context. Materialization proves only that files were
delivered. Every substantive consumer directive explicitly names and requires
reading the applicable canonical files before judgment or mutation; independent
reviewers and subagents likewise read their primary sources directly. Never create
`file_loaded`, `context_available`, hashes, manifests, epochs, or cache state to
pretend that delivery proves reading or understanding.

`process-id.txt` is a legitimate correlation between a workspace and a Moira
execution. It does not justify adjacent phases, ledgers, handoff protocols, or
copies of policy.

### Minimal consumed process record

Keep only process state that changes a later decision and has an identified writer and reader. A
node-local review outcome or immediate repair reach is justified when a condition or reviewer
consumes it. Pass IDs, proof tokens, ledgers, duplicated reports, and status matrices are not made
useful merely by being measurable.

### Workspace owner

Use one existing early responsibility to resolve the canonical workspace path.
When stable workspace files come from registry defaults, a shared `materialize`
node may create the directory and deliver them without copying their bodies
through agent context. Dynamic requirements, analyses, source captures, plans,
and reviews remain with the substantive owner that judges and writes them.
Mechanical setup is not a separate agent-directive responsibility.

### Source provenance and semantic reconciliation

Resolve all supported identities, preserve complete candidates, and compare
semantics before choosing a baseline. A merge is a designed reconciliation of
behavior and contracts, never a mechanical JSON combination.

### The reference the run writes itself

A body of criteria that outlives the step — planning rules, engineering principles, a review
contract — lives in `variableRegistry` as its single source. When `materialize` is available, deliver
that registry-backed document through the archive node so its rendered body does not enter agent
context; otherwise the first substantive workspace owner writes it alongside its other durable
sources. Every substantive later consumer, independent reviewers and subagents included, is told to read
the exact applicable canonical file or files before judgment or mutation. Materialization delivers
bytes but does not prove they were read, so the read obligation belongs in the consumer directive.

What decides the form is what the text is, not how many nodes touch it. An instruction the node
carries out now, in full, is part of that node's directive: an address for it would add a read and an
indirection for nothing. A document the run consults — navigated by section, returned to across
steps, read independently by roles with no shared context — needs an address.

This does not compete with static configuration; it continues it. The registry default remains the
single source either way. What changes with the size and role of the text is whether the run also
writes it down: a short rule a node applies whole stays configuration rendered into that directive,
while a body of criteria consulted across steps and by independent roles is configuration the run
also puts on disk. Neither form implies a manifest. Split a large body into stable thematic files when consumer groups
need different subjects; each shared rule still has exactly one canonical owner.

workflow_reference_review_repair.description: Canonical independent review, cause classification, repair, replan and reviewer contract
workflow_reference_review_repair.default:
# Moira workflow review and repair reference

## Review and repair

Use a cause-aware file-backed loop:

```text
produce-or-change -> independent review {pass | repair | replan}
                         | pass -> next
                         | repair -> repair owned artifact -> same review
                         | replan -> earliest invalid contract owner
```

The reviewer overwrites one known report file with the complete current set of
reproducible blocking findings and returns only the small aggregate route value.
Zero findings is `pass`. Classify each finding before mutation as a defect of the
reviewed artifact, a validation/test defect, insufficient existing evidence, a
documentation/projection defect, an invalid or unprovable criterion, or an
upstream requirements/plan/process defect. `repair` is valid only when every
blocker is owned by the reviewed artifact and its upstream contract remains
sound. Any upstream or evidence-model defect, including mixed findings, is
`replan`: the earliest invalid source wins.

The repair owner reads the report, reproduces defects, and either changes the
artifact or returns `reassess`. A changed repair supplies only bounded node-local
transition evidence that the next reviewer consumes: the root class and what
relevant source or reach actually changed. If it cannot reproduce the defect, the
proposed method cannot distinguish success from a plausible wrong state, or the
same root returns without stronger evidence, it must not start an unchanged loop.
It routes to contract reassessment instead.

A reviewer diagnoses but does not repair. It may block only on a violated
requirement, invalid engine construct, broken reachable route, lost required data,
unsafe side effect, unbounded loop, or required semantic guarantee that is
regressed/unverified. Naming taste, style preference, speculative robustness, and
hypothetical future needs are not blocking.

Do not build review algebra with pass IDs, active/frozen findings, resolution
matrices, multiple counters, reset branches, statuses, or intermediate reviews.
Collect all confirmed defects in the earliest failing tier in one pass; do not
reveal one issue per iteration. A repeat requires changed relevant knowledge: a
source of truth, external fact, discriminating observation, or testable
hypothesis. Changed bytes alone are insufficient. If recent cycles change only
validation or reporting infrastructure while the requested result and its direct
evidence do not improve, reassess the criterion and evidence model before another
mutation.

### File-backed review without data roundtrip

The report has a stable path. Reviewer returns only `pass`, `repair`, or `replan`; repair reads the
file. Findings and evidence are not copied into workflow context, so they survive the iteration that
produced them and stay readable by whoever repairs next, while context carries only the value a
condition needs.

### Cause before repair

Classify the earliest cause of a finding before choosing what to mutate. Only a confirmed defect
owned by the reviewed artifact authorizes automatic repair of that artifact. A validation defect,
insufficient evidence, an invalid or unprovable criterion, or an upstream requirements/plan/process
defect returns to its own contract owner. When causes are mixed, replan precedes repair so valid
implementation is not expanded against an invalid contract.

### Replan without requirement erosion

Replan is a normal quality-preserving result, not failure and not permission to lower the bar. It
corrects the earliest invalid derived interpretation, criterion, responsibility model, or evidence
method while preserving the user's original goal, scope, authority, and still-valid requirements.

### Bounded class-wide repair

A finding normally identifies a root class. Inspect every real manifestation of that confirmed root
inside the agreed scope and repair them coherently. This does not authorize a universal detection or
policy mechanism for a property whose truth remains contextual. The class is
bounded by confirmed cause and scope, not by every place where a newly invented mechanism could run.

### Routing a confirmed repair by its stale-evidence cone

A flow first classifies whether repair is legitimate. Only then does it send a confirmed repair back
to the earliest gate whose evidence could be stale.
That is right when the fix changed behaviour and absurd when it corrected a sentence in a test name,
and paying the whole chain for a one-line correction is not merely slow: it teaches the run to batch
findings until a round feels worth the chain, and it tempts the author to delete gates that were
earning their cost.

The construct that resolves it is one answer and one case on the node that gives it. The repair
owner declares a required enum as a node-local property — not a registry global, so the answer
cannot outlive the transition that routes on it — and states, after the repair, where the
correction actually landed: `contained` when it stayed inside what that gate judges and the
project's own deterministic checks over what changed have been run and passed, `spreading`
otherwise. The same node carries the case: `contained` selects the connection back to the gate that
raised the finding, and `success` — the output taken when no case holds — is the full chain, so the
conservative route is the one an unexpected answer takes. A separate condition node is right only
when several repair owners share that routing.

Three things keep it honest. Reach describes what the change touched rather than how much the finding
mattered: a severity tier invites an argument about importance, while a reach answer can be checked
against the diff that was just made. It is stated by whoever made the correction, after making it,
because before the repair nobody knows what the fix will touch — least of all a reviewer, which never
sees the repair when it is delegated, and which would in any case be deciding how much revalidation
its own findings deserve, the one judgement its independence does not extend to. And the
deterministic checks are what stand in for the skipped chain, so a repair that turned out larger than
it looked takes the long route whatever it looked like when it started.

The short route is not an exemption from the gate. It returns there, and that gate confirms closure
before the run moves on; this is how a flow establishes which gates actually went stale, not a way of
passing the ones that did. If the repair cannot name changed relevant knowledge, route to reassessment
rather than treating changed bytes as a reason to repeat.

## Reviewer contract

Review the artifact as executed by the real engine, under the loop and the blocking bar already
stated in `Review and repair`. What belongs to the role itself: for a proposed field, identify its
writer, its reader, and its runtime effect; for a removed node, locate its responsibilities,
evidence, conditions, and routes; verify that mutations return through the gates whose evidence they
invalidated, that repeats rest on changed evidence, that expensive checks are conditional and
ordered, and that side effects are authorized. A finding is a defect you can reproduce in the
artifact, never a design you would have preferred.

workflow_reference_validation.description: Canonical validation evidence modalities, discriminating observations, structural projection and cost ordering
workflow_reference_validation.default:
# Moira workflow validation reference

## Validation and cost ordering

Fail first by prerequisites and cost, not by hiding later findings:

```text
identity/access/provenance
-> cheap deterministic structural checks
-> applicable runtime checks
-> applicable expensive checks
-> semantic review
-> finalization and authorized side effects
```

Converge cheaper mutating gates before broad expensive validation. A late mutation
returns through the earliest gate whose evidence became stale. Do not rerun checks
that cannot diagnose or change the failure. Preserve conditional skip behavior
when consolidating nodes; absorbed browser, integration, performance, compilation,
or full-test work must not become unconditional.

Judge a refactor by semantic retention first: a required guarantee that is regressed or unverified
blocks acceptance, whatever else improved. Cost is read afterwards and separately — turns spent
without judgement, references rendered again for readers that already hold them, state nobody
consumes, checks repeated where they cannot diagnose — and never folded into one score that lets an
improvement pay for lost behaviour. Runtime token or latency claims remain unverified without real
telemetry.

Task-first discovery replaces mandatory onboarding ceremony. Read only context
needed for the current goal. Create an optional concise workspace context artifact
when it will have real consumers; do not require permanent policy generation before
ordinary work. Reconsider scaffolding inherited from older, weaker model
generations: fixed search counts, filename recipes, prescribed plan forms, tool
sequences, and microsteps need a current contract or reproduced failure.

### Discriminating evidence and matching modality

Before making a check contractual, name the required state, a plausible wrong state that can look
similar, and the observation that reliably differs between them. If the same observation can occur
in both states, it is not evidence for that property. Do not create a surrogate proof; use an
appropriate behavioral, architectural, independent, or user judgment, or correct the criterion.

Match the evidence method to the property. Registry, schema, and identifier completeness can often
be checked mechanically. Semantic scenario completeness and the business provenance of a result
cannot be inferred merely from an operational surrogate that the wrong state can reproduce.
Conversely, do not replace a reliable deterministic check with subjective review.

### Validation as a requested result

Validation infrastructure is legitimate when it is itself part of the requested outcome, has a real
consumer, and produces an observation that distinguishes relevant states. Otherwise validation is
supporting evidence and must remain subordinate to the requested result. A check must not generate a
separate system whose purpose is proving that the check or another validator ran.

### Current structural projection before topology judgment

When a complete workflow artifact exists, generate one complete, addressable structural projection
with the official environment tool before judging topology or data flow. The responsibility that
selects, creates, or changes the artifact owns the projection for that exact revision and refreshes
the same canonical file before handing the revision to another role. Analysis and independent review
use the projection to see the whole node and edge corpus, reachability classes, cycles, dangling
targets, and declared data flow, then inspect the complete workflow definition for conditions,
directives, authority, and semantic meaning.

The projection is derived evidence, not a second source of truth, a validator, or proof that another
agent read or understood the workflow. Do not add a freshness flag, checksum protocol, proof token,
or validator for the projection. Freshness is distinguished by rendering the current artifact and
comparing the actual structural content at the canonical address. Before the first complete create
artifact exists, review the explicit graph design contract; do not require an impossible projection.

workflow_reference_authority.description: Canonical user authority, operating-mode and external side-effect boundaries for workflows
workflow_reference_authority.default:
# Moira workflow authority reference

## Authority and side effects

Tool availability is not authorization. Publication, external mutations,
destructive operations, environment changes, and administrative overrides require
the user's task or explicit approval. Different user choices must cause observably
different routes or request semantics.

Honor an already explicit decision without asking it again or deliberately making
a known-to-fail attempt. Preserve error recovery for genuinely new failures. Do not
persist retry flags or build a state machine around one request; route the concrete
failure to its owner.

### Operating mode (autonomous vs interactive)

A workflow that a caller may want to run unattended declares exactly one registry global
`operating_mode` with `enum: ["autonomous", "interactive"]`. The first node that already talks
to the user resolves it in the same turn — never a separate turn whose only output is that
value. Its directive must reuse a mode the user already stated, infer an unambiguous one
(including running as a child of an already autonomous process), and otherwise ask once while
naming the consequence. The mode is never re-asked later.

A `condition` on that global precedes each user-approval gate and sends the autonomous branch to
the node the gate reaches on approval; the gate keeps its directive, schema and interactive
routes, including rejection loops. Retarget every incoming edge of a gated node to its
condition, or a back edge will still stop an autonomous run.

Autonomous mode removes only waits for a human: approvals, acceptances, feedback prompts, and
decisions the agent can derive. It never removes independent agent reviews, validation, replan
or recovery routes, and it never removes an authority gate: publication, destructive operations
and external mutations stay user-authorized, and in autonomous mode such a node resolves to the
safe answer without asking instead of being routed away. The user still receives a final report
in both modes, so an autonomous branch needs a report responsibility where the interactive one
both reports and asks.

Do not add statuses, counters, `*_skipped` flags, duplicate mode aliases, or a mode question
inside each gate. An `inputSchema` cannot branch on a context variable, so mode handling is
route-based, not schema-based.

workflow_reference_patterns.default:
# Moira workflow authoring patterns

The patterns are split by complexity tier. Each sits in the lowest tier where it applies, and a flow
uses its own tier's section and every section below it. The complex tier adds no patterns of its
own: a complex flow uses every pattern here together with the design, review-repair and validation
references.

## Simple tier

### Straight-line default

Start with a linear graph: every node is a turn the agent pays for, and every branch is a decision a
later reader has to justify. Add a branch only for a real alternative outcome, and a repair loop only
when changing the reviewed artifact can resolve the finding — a loop that cannot fix its own cause
repeats the work and hides the real blocker.

### Routing on the answer

A step that returns a verdict routes on it: an enum answer in `inputSchema`, one case per outcome
that leaves the ordinary path, `success` for the ordinary one, and a folded `expressions` entry for
the counter the verdict is compared with. The reviewer, the approval gate and the retry budget are
then one node each, and the process view shows one labelled transition per outcome instead of a
chain of checks. Reach for a separate condition only for the cases the design reference names — a
shared decision, state no single node produced, a decision point the reader should see by name.

### Verifiable completion conditions

A completion condition names a result someone other than the agent could observe: a file that
exists, a message the user received, a value the step returned, a check that passed. "The task is
done" or "the agent understood" describes an intention, so nothing can accept or refuse it, and the
step completes whether or not the work happened. Write each condition so that reading the result is
enough to say whether it holds.

### Questions that explain and argue

Wherever the workflow's agent asks the person something — an approval, a choice, a missing fact —
its directive tells it to explain the question in the person's terms: what each option means and
what follows from choosing it. When the agent proposes an answer, it says which one it recommends and
why, from what it knows about this run, so the person agrees or disagrees for a reason instead of
guessing. The person still decides; the explanation lets them decide knowingly. In an autonomous run
the same reasons go into the report of the decision the agent took. When several gates of one
workflow ask in the same way, one shared playbook can carry the explanation instead of a copy in each
directive.

### Minimal workflow editing

Use the official API or CLI required by the active environment. Validate the real artifact. Do not
introduce a one-off generator, migrator, intermediate format, or hidden runtime dependency merely to
make the edit: each becomes an undeclared dependency, so the workflow round-trips correctly only
where that tool exists and nothing in the definition says so.

## Standard tier

### Behaviour text belongs in a playbook, not in a directive

A rule about *how* the agent should behave — a review standard, a tone of voice, a definition of
done — is not part of what the process does. Keep it in a playbook and name it from the node:
`\{{playbook:review-standard}}` for your own, `\{{playbook:@owner/name}}` for somebody else's
published one. The reference resolves at every step, so editing the playbook changes behaviour
without touching the graph, and the same text can serve several workflows instead of being copied
into each.

Keep a `variableRegistry` default for text that belongs to this workflow alone and changes with it.
Reach for a playbook when the text is reused, or when someone who does not edit workflows should be
able to change it.

A reference to a playbook the author cannot read is refused while editing and before a run starts;
if one becomes unreadable mid-run, the step continues with a visible placeholder and the run records
that it ran without that text.

## Complex tier

No additional patterns: see the note above.

workflow_reference_antipatterns.description: Canonical workflow defect catalog for complete semantic audits and reviews
workflow_reference_antipatterns.default:
# Moira workflow authoring antipatterns

The catalog is split by complexity tier. Each entry sits in the lowest tier where it applies, and a
flow is checked against its own tier's section and every section below it: a simple flow against the
simple section, a standard flow against simple and standard, a complex flow against all three.

- **Simple** — defects a short flow of steps in order, with at most one choice or one approval, can
  actually have.
- **Standard** — design, review, repair and edit discipline for flows with real branches,
  review-and-redo loops, approvals, durable files or side effects under the user's authority.
- **Complex** — evidence, validation and replanning machinery for flows with several interacting
  loops, sub-processes, teleports, locks, multi-stage progress or high-authority effects.

## Simple tier

### Avoidable routing scaffolding

A `condition` node whose only job is to route on the answer the preceding node just returned, or an
`expression` node whose only job is to count what that node already knows, adds a hop the reader
must follow and a second place the decision lives. Fold it: the deciding node carries the `cases`
(and the `expressions`) and routes itself; `success` carries the ordinary outcome. The tell is a
routing node with one incoming connection whose condition reads only that node's outputs. Keep the
separate node only for the cases the design reference names — a shared decision, state no single
node produced, a named decision point the reader needs, a computation with its own place.

### State without a consumer

Every field needs a clear writer, named reader, and concrete routing/rendering effect. Remove it if
any part is missing: state nobody reads still has to be produced, kept true, and reasoned about by
every later reader, and the first time it goes stale nothing catches it.

### Decorative flags, statuses, result codes, and evidence

`done`, `success`, `*_created`, `*_fixed`, result codes, pass numbers, and evidence
that merely restate a successful transition are invalid. A short bounded evidence
field is justified only when a later participant truly consumes the fact.

### False variation

Do not ask users to choose among values that reach the same behavior. Choices must have observable
consequences: a question whose answers converge spends the user's decision on nothing and teaches
them the questions are decorative, which costs you the answers you actually need later.

### Declaration/route mismatch

Every schema-allowed response must have a correct reachable outcome, and conditional feedback or
failure data must be required when their route consumes them. Otherwise a schema-valid answer has
nowhere to go: the run stalls, or takes a route that contradicts what the agent just said.

### Procedural fragmentation

Do not create agent turns only to create a directory, copy/rename a report, relay known data, count
items, assemble a prompt, collect a known path, write another agent's result, or present it without
new judgment. Every relay turn is a place where the work can be misreported while nobody adds
judgement, and the owner's own account of it becomes second-hand. Combine action and its durable
report under the substantive owner.

### Unauthorized side effects

Never publish, delete, overwrite, switch external context, or perform another
mutation merely because a tool permits it.

### Directive as a drill order

A directive spells out the sequence of moves an executor would derive from the goal on its own,
or raises its voice to make a rule stick — capitals, warning signs, MANDATORY, NEVER, CRITICAL,
FIX IT, NO REPORTS — and usually does both.

Volume adds no executability. There is no state of the world in which "do this ACTUALLY critically"
holds or fails, so nothing can accept or refuse it, and the executor is left performing the form
instead of judging the work. The steps have the same problem from the other side: they are right
only for the case the author pictured, and the executor that meets a different one either follows
them into the wrong result or ignores the directive entirely, having learned that its words are
decoration.

Two signs, and each finds cases the other misses. Remove the capitals and the signs: if the rule
stops requiring anything, there was no requirement, only tone. Or read the steps and ask whether an
executor holding the goal would have arrived at them anyway — a directive built as "STEP 1 …
STEP 2 …" can be quiet and still be a drill order.

### A bare question or an unargued proposal

A directive that asks the person to choose, approve or confirm without telling the agent to explain
the options and what follows from each, or that lets the agent put forward a recommendation without
its reasons. The same defect in an autonomous run is a decision the agent takes on the person's
behalf without recording why. The person answers blind, or later reads a decision they cannot
follow: they approve what they do not understand or refuse what they would have accepted, and the
result of the run rests on a guess. The fix is in the directive: name what each option means for the
person, and have the agent state its recommendation, or its decision, with the reasons from this run.

### Optimizing for node count

Do not choose a desired number and delete toward it. First preserve responsibilities
and guarantees, then observe the resulting size.

### Hidden runtime in temporary tools

Do not make a one-off script or intermediate representation an undeclared dependency of the
workflow. A workflow that needs it works only where it exists, and the definition gives the next
author no hint that anything is missing.

## Standard tier

### Reimplementing the workflow engine

Do not add run IDs, phases, internal state machines, locks, hashes, manifests,
ledgers, transactions, or deduplication without a proven requirement not covered
by the engine. Locks themselves are valid when actual concurrency/ownership
requires the engine's lock node; decorative locking protocols are not.

### Mechanical validation over the validator

Do not model `validation_passed`, error lists, reset expressions, retry counters,
and limit branches for rules already enforced by the engine, API, or official CLI.
The mutation owner fixes concrete validator errors before completing.

### Late design discovery

The first independent examination of acceptance, responsibility, authority, or evidence semantics
happens only after implementation. Review then becomes the strongest specification and repeatedly
co-authors omissions that the design and producer should have handled before handoff.

### User approval as semantic review

A user's preference or authorization decision is treated as independent correctness evidence.
Human approval remains important for authority and product choice, but semantic design review is a
separate responsibility and must precede it when the workflow promises independent quality.

### Engine state computed by the agent

A workflow that genuinely needs a number — the round of evidence in progress, a cursor, a total —
declares it in the registry and lets an expression on the route compute it: an `expressions` entry
on the node that has the evidence, or an `expression` node when the computation stands alone. What must not
happen is asking a node to produce a value the engine could have derived from state it already holds,
such as the next number of a counter the registry owns.

The boundary is who holds the inputs, not whether arithmetic happened. A count of findings the
reviewer just made, or the number of units in a plan the agent just wrote, is derived from material
only that agent has read, and it belongs in its answer. A value whose inputs the engine already has
does not.

The consequence is a path nobody can write down. On the turn of the node that is about to return the
next value, the variable still holds the previous one, so a directive telling that node where to
write cannot render the directory it is creating. It degenerates into "write it there", the agent
supplies a file name of its own, and no later reader knows where to look — while the number itself
arrives as a claim rather than a fact. Move the computation onto the route and the same directive
renders exactly.

The tell is a value in `globalInputs` that the engine could compute from what it already holds, and,
beside it, a directive that describes a path instead of naming one.

### Duplicate source of truth

Do not store the same detailed content in a file, an output, another field/file, and a rendered
prompt. Copies drift the moment one of them is updated, and a reader has no way to tell which is
current. Keep it once and pass only genuine route values.

### Review-loop algebra

Do not add pass IDs, statuses, frozen findings, resolution matrices, counters,
reset branches, or several reviewers around the ordinary review loop without a
separate observable policy requiring them.

### Unchanged or unbounded repetition

Every repeat needs a changed artifact/input/state or new hypothesis. If repair
cannot change or reproduce the defect, escalate the factual cause instead of
looping. Do not add counters merely to make an otherwise ordinary review loop look
bounded.

### Mixed validation and repair

An independent validator diagnoses; a separate repair owner mutates; the same validator reviews the
changed artifact again. When one node does both, nothing independent confirms the fix and the report
describes the state before the change.

### Mutation after final gate

Every mutation of the final artifact occurs before final gates or returns through
all gates whose evidence it invalidates.

### Premature authoritative derived data

Counts and summaries are not authoritative while their source can still change.
Do not route or message from derived values before the source is approved.

### Duplicate aliases

Use one canonical value. With two names for it, every writer must remember both and a reader cannot
tell which one the routes actually read. An alias needs a proven external compatibility contract.

### Abstraction without reuse

Do not create a child workflow, subgraph, adapter, or protocol only to hide local complexity. The
complexity survives the move and is now split across two definitions with a mapping between them, so
both must be read to understand either. Abstraction needs an independent reusable contract.

### Reviewer designing machinery

A reviewer proves defects in the agreed artifact. It does not add fields,
protocols, loops, or abstraction layers for possible future robustness.

### Reviewer required to find an issue

Zero blocking findings is normal. After repair, targeted rereview may accept the
artifact; it must not search indefinitely for a new reason to expand scope.

### Reviewer without the engine model

Before proposing coordination machinery, verify execution order, output scopes,
transition rules, persistence, and actual concurrency.

### Project-specific policy made universal

Do not embed one VCS, CI, directory layout, command, UI, test framework, or docs
policy into a general workflow. Discover applicable local rules.

### Bulk change without responsibility tracing

Before removing a concept, inspect definitions, all uses, incoming/outgoing edges, artifacts,
failure/skip routes, and external contracts. A concept removed only from the places a plan lists
takes its routes, artifacts, and skip conditions with it silently, and the loss surfaces later as a
run that ends in the wrong place.

### Planning an edit blind to the source's own defects

An edit is planned against the requested change alone while the source already carries defects nobody
looked for. The plan then repairs one thing correctly and the workflow keeps failing for reasons that
were visible all along, usually surfacing on a later run as unrelated breakage.

Auditing the complete source against the known catalog is what makes those defects visible. Whether
that audit runs, and which of its findings join the scope, is the user's decision — it is their time
and their scope — not a step the flow takes on its own or a question it repeats after the scope is
settled.

### Partial, remembered, or stale workflow topology

Topology or data-flow judgment is made from named nodes, selected reads, remembered routes, a green
validator result, or a projection produced for an earlier artifact revision. A middle branch,
teleport-only entry, distant data consumer, or repaired connection can then be omitted even though
the inspected fragments look correct. Require the one current complete structural projection when a
complete artifact exists, and confirm semantic meaning in the complete definition. Do not answer
this defect by creating a second abbreviated graph, an invocation receipt, or proof machinery for
the reviewer.

### A reference with no address

A body of criteria that outlives the step is carried only as text rendered into node directives, so
it has no address anywhere.

The first consequence is that a reader needing one section receives the whole body, again on every
visit, although nothing in it changed since the run began. The second is worse: a reader outside the
run's context cannot be given the text at all, because a subagent never sees the parent's directive.
The parent then starts copying the body into a prompt, and the same criteria live in two places that
drift apart.

The defect is the missing address; repeated delivery is only its symptom. What an auditor notices is
one registry variable interpolated by unrelated responsibilities, or a directive that assembles a
prompt out of content the workflow already owns.

### Materialized doctrine duplicated in directives

A workflow materializes canonical guidance and then repeats the same rule, literally or in
paraphrase, inside consumer directives. The copies drift, enlarge prompts, and make ownership
ambiguous. Keep shared doctrine in exactly one thematic reference. A consumer directive names and
requires reading the applicable file, while retaining only its local inputs, output, authority,
routing, and failure contract. Materialization alone is not evidence that the file was read.

### Legacy capability scaffolding

Do not retain ceremony solely because older models needed it. Fixed searches,
onboarding chains, forced plan templates, and decomposed mechanical turns require a
current observable benefit.

### Order of telling taken for order of work

A list of tasks written by a person is a record of thinking, not a queue. The condition the first
item depends on is often realised while writing the third and written down there; a remark that
governs the whole job lands in the middle and looks like another item. A numbered list reads as an
instruction about order, and that appearance is the only reason it is taken for one.

A flow that freezes the written sequence as the execution sequence therefore produces work done
without a stated precondition, and a rework its author never asked for. The two things a directive
must keep apart are what the items say and in which order they run. Content and completeness belong
to whoever wrote the list, and a flow is right to forbid rewriting an item, dropping one, or
enriching it with work nobody asked for. The order belongs to the executor, who is the one that can
see item two cannot start until item three exists.

The defect appears when one prohibition covers both at once, and the usual carrier is the word
renumber: it reads as "do not restate the items under new numbers" and equally as "do not work out
which runs first", so forbidding it hands back the content and takes the ordering with it.
Reordering is not an operation on content — it is the ordering, the thing the paragraph above
leaves with the executor. A directive that means to protect the list says so in terms of the items
themselves.

## Complex tier

### Non-discriminating evidence

A proposed signal is compatible with both the required state and a plausible wrong state, yet is
reported as proof. The defect is causal: the observation does not distinguish the claim.

### Evidence modality mismatch

A structural or operational fact is used to prove semantic completeness, architectural fitness, or
business provenance; or subjective review replaces a reliable mechanical property. Choose evidence
from the property, not from whichever tool is easiest to automate.

### Repair before diagnosis

Every finding automatically authorizes mutation of the reviewed artifact. This confuses a result
defect with a broken validator, insufficient evidence, documentation projection, invalid criterion,
or upstream plan/process defect and expands implementation against a contract that may be wrong.

### Validator nesting

A new mechanism exists mainly to prove that another check ran, produced a report, or used the desired
path. The new mechanism creates another proof obligation and then demands proof of that obligation.
Stop when the validation layer is not an independently
requested result with a consumer and discriminating outcome.

### Changed bytes without changed knowledge

A review loop repeats because files changed even though the relevant source of truth, hypothesis,
and distinguishing observation did not. Additional surrogate machinery cannot close
the same-root finding when they add no stronger evidence.

### Universal detector for a contextual property

Class-wide repair is interpreted as permission to build a general scanner or framework for a
property whose truth depends on architecture, semantics, or business context. Inspect bounded real
manifestations of a confirmed root instead of replacing judgment with an unsound universal surrogate.

### Validation-only drift

Successive cycles change only validation, reporting, or acceptance machinery while
the requested result and its direct evidence do not improve. Reassess the criterion and proof model
before allowing another validation-only mutation.

### Repeating irrelevant checks

Return a failure to the closest owner of its cause. Do not rerun broad validation
because an unchanged external finalization request failed.

### Wrong cost order and validation amplification

Do not run expensive/environment-dependent checks before cheap prerequisites, or
repeat full suites after a small later-iteration change when targeted evidence can
stabilize the artifact first. Preserve project policy and risk-based full gates;
avoid validation work whose evidence is already current outside the mutation cone.

### Lost conditionality

Consolidation must preserve applicability, order, failure, and skip semantics. Do
not make all absorbed checks unconditional.

### Fixed semantic quality score

Do not reduce architecture, completeness, testability, or semantic retention to a
threshold score. Required guarantees are hard gates; cost diagnostics remain
separate and cannot compensate for regression.


The same defect arrives as a minimum: a count of sources, of alternatives, of decision records, of
test cases. What separates a requirement from a fabricated threshold is where the number comes
from. A bound that an external contract imposes — a contrast ratio a standard requires, a retention
a regulation sets — states an obligation, and its violation is observable outside the run. A bound
invented inside the workflow does not distinguish two states of the result: the difference between
seven sources and eight says nothing about whether the research answers its question, and it is met
by adding the eighth. Ask what the neighbouring value would mean; if nothing, the number is
standing in for the reading nobody did.

### Plan as a mechanical implementation script

A plan fixes outcomes, mandatory invariants, contracts, known dependencies,
acceptance evidence, and material risks. It does not impose exact commands,
microsteps, exhaustive file/node lists, pseudocode, or one edit tactic without an
external reason. Reviewer blocks missing contracts and unjustified constraints,
not harmless implementation freedom.


Where the deliverable is itself prose — a document, a set of subagent briefs, the answer of an
investigation, a body of rules — the plan and the result are written in the same medium, and
nothing separates them by construction. A plan item then grows until it contains the deliverable,
the review of the plan reviews the result, and the step that was supposed to execute it is reduced
to copying text into a file. The test that holds in any medium is whether work an intelligent
executor still has to do remains after the plan is approved. Prescriptions phrased for code —
"no file paths, no symbols, no pseudocode" — do not detect this: the prose plan names no files
and is the result anyway.

### Redundancy required in every plan item

The problem this rule answers is real: an executor often receives one item with the rest of the plan
absent from its context, so an item that leans on "as above" is unexecutable. The rule as usually
written answers it unconditionally — repeat every nuance, duplicate every cross-cutting action into
every item, redundancy is required and never a smell.

Two consequences follow. The item grows until it carries the deliverable, which is the plan-as-a-
script defect arriving through the front door. And the repeated text becomes a duplicate source of
truth, with the drift that entry already describes, now mandated by a rule instead of happening by
accident. The form that keeps the benefit states what the executor needs when it is alone —
the goal the item serves, the constraints and evidence for that item — and leaves duplication to be
judged item by item, on whether it genuinely applies there.
