# Moira workflow progress reference

## The process view

A workflow of more than one stage declares `progress` by default: the process a person reads
without knowing the graph. Leaving it out is allowed only with a reason recorded in the design or
edit plan — a flow of a single step, say. Why: the run page and the overview of a person's runs
show exactly what the flow declares, and a flow without blocks is shown as a run with no
progress to report. Its `nodes` array is the list of **blocks** in process order; each
block carries a label and a one-sentence description in `content.summary`, with optional
`details`, `outcome` and `next`. The view is derived from the executable graph, never drawn
beside it, so it cannot drift from what runs. The rules below are outcomes; a rule that does not
apply to the current change is met and needs nothing produced to prove it.

- **Every node belongs to one block.** Each node of the primary graph — routing nodes (`start`,
  `condition`, `expression`), notifications and terminals included — declares the block it
  belongs to through `progressNodeId`. Why: a run is projected from the route it took; a node
  outside every block is work the picture cannot show, and a routing node placed in the block
  whose decision it routes is what makes a skipped block visibly skipped.
- **Every block is described.** `content.summary` is mandatory and says what the stage does in
  one sentence a newcomer understands; the label names the stage as a person would. Why: the
  block is the unit the reader sees first; a bare label is a heading without a paragraph.
- **Every boundary edge is labelled.** A connection that leaves its block, and a connection
  that loops back inside a block, carries a `connectionLabels` entry keyed like `connections`:
  a short phrase naming the decision ("plan approved", "review found defects"). Why: the
  arrows between blocks are the process; an unlabelled arrow makes the reader open the graph.
- **Every return explains itself.** A transition to an earlier block or to its own block is a
  loop; its label is an object `{ "label": …, "cycle": { "cause": …, "exit": … } }` naming
  what causes the repetition and what ends it. Why: loops are where newcomers lose the thread;
  the cause and the exit are the two facts that make a loop readable and bounded.
- **Process order reads left to right.** Array order is process order; a transition to a
  lower index is a return. A block that several blocks lead into (a hub — replan, stop) is
  placed after the blocks that feed it. Why: the order is the only sequence the reader has.
- **The array is bounded and its order is the only order.** The schema caps `progress.nodes`
  (`maxItems`, 18 today); a process with more stages groups them into fewer blocks a newcomer
  can hold. The earlier model's display order, `progress.nodes[].connections.default`, is still
  accepted by the validator (it must name an existing block) but plays no part in the derived
  process, whose order and transitions come from array order and the labelled connections; an
  author need not write it. Why: two orders would have to agree, and only one of them is what
  the engine draws and validates.
- **One outcome owner per result.** An outcome template `{{progress_*_outcome}}` sits on
  exactly one block, and that block owns a node whose `globalInputs` write the variable; other
  blocks may also write it. Why: the block that shows a result must be one where the result is
  produced, or the picture claims a conclusion it never reached.

- **A block that works through a list binds it.** When the flow keeps the list a stage works
  through in its variables — items, a cursor, a finished count, a total — the block declares
  `list: { items?, title?, current?, done?, total?, indexBase? }` with the variable paths, and
  the run shows the items, done/total and the current item, the time spent on each, and the
  count in every notification. Nothing in the binding names a plan or a checklist: the block says
  what it counts, the run supplies the values; counters alone (`current` and `total`) suffice
  when no items array exists. The CLI sets it with `edit-block <id> --list '<json>'` and
  `--list none` removes it; the validator refuses a path whose root is neither a declared global
  nor a node id, and a `title` without `items`. Why: a stage that says "unit 3 of 5, Wire the
  CLI" is read at a glance, and typical durations per item can only be gathered when the run
  knows which item a pass worked on.
- **Every block is connected.** Each block has at least one transition to or from another block;
  a self-return alone connects nothing; the block that owns the start node is exempt. Why: a block
  that nothing reaches and that reaches nothing is a stage the picture shows but the run can never
  be in, so the reader is told a step that does not exist.

The engine enforces the mechanical half of these rules at validation, each violation an error
with a stable code: `unowned-node`, `unknown-block`, `empty-block`, `empty-description`,
`unlabeled-edge`, `unexplained-cycle`, `outcome-duplicate`, `outcome-unowned`,
`unconnected-block`. The official CLI
authors the contract one change at a time — `set-block <node> <block>`, `add-block`,
`edit-block`, `set-label <node> <key> <text> [--cause … --exit …]`, `clear-label` — and
`derive` prints the derived process: blocks with their nodes, labelled transitions, returns
with cause and exit, hubs, and every diagnostic — the nine above and `no-start`, which only
`derive` reports: without a start node the blocks and transitions are still listed, but the
walk that finds returns inside a block cannot run, so only returns to an earlier block are
flagged until a start exists. A producer completes with zero diagnostics;
the reviewer reads `derive` as the process projection and judges what the validator cannot:
whether each label is true to the condition or branch it annotates, whether each cycle names
the real cause and exit, whether the descriptions and the order read as the process a newcomer
would recognise.

## Steps that wait for a person

A step where the flow asks the person for a decision and waits for it — approve a plan, accept a
result, choose how to continue past a blocker — declares `humanGate` on its `agent-directive`:
`{ "label": …, "when": …, "notify": "auto" | "off", "remindAfter": "30m" | "4h" | "1d" }`. While
a run is paused there it is shown as **waiting for you** rather than waiting for the agent, and
the person is told. The mark changes nothing the agent sees: directive, input and routing stay
as they are. The CLI sets it with `update <node> --human-gate '<json>'` and removes it with
`--human-gate none`; `schema`, `structure` and `diff` show it.

- **Mark by meaning, not by wording.** The step waits for the person when its directive asks
  them and the run cannot go on without their answer. A step the agent decides by itself is not
  marked. A step where the agent does long work first and asks only at the end is not marked
  either — it would read «waiting for you» during the work; its directive has the agent raise
  `session await-user` when it asks, which shows the wait and tells the person. Why: the mark is how
  a person finds, among many runs, the ones whose next move is theirs.
- **A step the autonomous mode also enters carries `when`.** When an autonomous run reaches the
  same step and decides it without asking, `when` is the condition under which the step waits for
  the person — typically `{ "operator": "neq", "left": { "contextPath": "operating_mode" },
  "right": "autonomous" }`. It is evaluated as the run arrives. A step that autonomous runs route
  around needs no `when`. Why: without it an autonomous run shows «waiting for you» where nobody
  is waited for.
- **One message per wait.** With `notify: "auto"` (the default) the engine sends the person a
  message on arrival: the task, the label and a link to the run. When the flow already sends its
  own `user-notification` right before the step — usually because that message carries what the
  person decides on (the plan, the result, the reason for a blocker) — the step sets
  `notify: "off"`: the flow's message is the first message and the engine does not repeat it.
  The validator warns (`gate-notified-twice`) about a notification that leads straight into a
  step that notifies itself.
- **A wait that may last gets a reminder.** `remindAfter` makes the engine send one reminder
  with a link to the run when the wait lasts that long, with either `notify` value. It counts from
  when the run started waiting there (or, for a run already there when the step is marked, from
  that update).

## The overview of a person's runs

The overview shows every unfinished run as a card built only from what the flow declares: the
blocks become the row of stages and the list of stages, a block's bound `list` becomes the plan
items with the current one, and `humanGate` becomes «waiting for you» with its label. A flow that
declares none of this still appears, but its card has nothing to say about progress.

## Execution task identity

Every workflow establishes a concise human-readable name of the actual user's task through
Progress/session at its first evidence-bearing intake responsibility, before completing intake.
An intake reached before workspace materialization uses the already available runtime API; it
does not require a reference file that a later node has not delivered. Later authoring and
scope-change responsibilities read this canonical guidance after delivery. A name describes
the task, separately from the workflow's own name, the current step, its result and arbitrary notes.

Read session({ action: "execution_context", executionId }) for the current process. Persist the
name with session({ action: "update-task-title", executionId, taskTitle, expectedRevision,
expectedTaskIdentityRevision }), using its revision and metadataRevisions.taskIdentity.
Use trimmed nonempty plain text of at most 500 characters without forbidden controls. The
authenticated execution owner can create or rename identity on an active run; finished runs
refuse changes. A stale response requires a fresh authoritative read and reconciliation of the
actual task before another rename, never a blind replay or a continuation-guard bypass.

The server owns taskIdentity and its change time/token. The operation does not consume the
presented Step attempt, advance the step generation, clear the person's question or alter context,
parent or reminder revisions. An identical normalized title leaves metadata revision, activity and
events unchanged; a real rename contributes meaningful activity. Do not write naming into
variables, notes, node responses as a competing source, or a copied metadata object.

When the actual task changes during requirement revision, replanning or contract reassessment,
the responsibility that holds the new scope updates the same identity before completing its new
contract. A change only to implementation tactics does not require a rename. Producers and
independent reviewers judge that the authored intake and real scope-change owners perform this
effect; merely suggesting a future call does not establish the name.

Canonical headings use explicit runtime identity first, then the resolved authored progress
title, then the run's own workflow name. They never extract a title from execution.note.
Existing runs without identity retain this truthful fallback. A workflow without an authored
progress graph still supports execution identity; identity alone invents no process or blocks.
Notes remain separately inspectable arbitrary text. Notifications and progress representations
consume the same canonical heading; messages already delivered retain their historical name.

## Content and rendering

Use the canonical execution task identity, a bounded template `goal`, generic `facts` such as
mode or attention, and block content rendered through the normal protected template processor
over declared workflow variables only. Definition and resolved output bounds apply; content is
plain escaped text. An exact waiting node may override the active block's label and content
through `progressActiveLabel` and `progressActiveContent`; the override applies only while that
node is current, and `progressActiveContent` shallowly replaces only the supplied `summary`,
`details`, `outcome` or `next` fields. All essential information is immediately readable in
the Web UI and in the PNG; no required meaning exists only on hover.

The producer that owns a semantic result also owns its outcome text. A plan or process
revision atomically replaces the current revision, obsolete future units, counters, activity
and next action while retaining only still-true completed outcomes. Do not add progress
conditions, status, history, cursor, proof tokens, runtime protocols, or a separately
maintained layout or state graph: the run's state comes from the engine.

## How a run is shown

The engine records every execution's route — each node it ran, the connection it left through
(a teleport as a `teleport` exit), the variables it changed, and where it waited — and projects
the run onto the process from that route, never from block order: the block of the last visit
is `active`, or `waiting` when the run pauses there; a visited block is `done`, or `repeated`
with the number of passes through its working steps; a block whose work never ran or that the
run bypassed is `skipped`; the rest are `pending`. Two cases decide `skipped`: an unvisited
block that lies before the furthest visited block in process order was passed by the run and
is `skipped`, while an unvisited block after it is `pending`; and a block where only its routing
nodes ran is `skipped`, unless the block consists of routing nodes alone, whose routing is its
work and reads as `done`. Why: the picture must say "the run went around this" and "the run
has not got here yet" differently, and a routing-only block (a mode switch, a gate) has done
its job when it routed. Nothing unvisited is ever shown as done. A
value set from outside the flow appears as a runtime adjustment with its actor. An execution
recorded before routes existed shows only its current block and `routeRecorded: false`.
Design the blocks so that this projection tells the truth: a repair loop inside one block reads
as that block repeated, a bypassed approval reads as skipped, a stop reads as its own block.

## Review

Mechanical validation proves schema, ownership, labels and template references; primary-artifact
review judges semantic usefulness, scenario completeness and business provenance. Reviewers
reject append-only stale summaries, mixed revisions, undeclared template references, labels
that contradict their conditions, cycles without a real cause or exit, orders that do not read
as the process, arbitrary HTML, or engine fields tied to one workflow domain.

Three findings block, each judged from the directives and the graph rather than from wording:

1. A workflow of more than one stage without `progress` and without a recorded reason.
2. A step that asks the person for a decision and waits for it without `humanGate` (or, for a
   step that works first and asks at the end, without a directive to raise `session await-user`); and
   the reverse — a `humanGate` on a step that an autonomous run enters and decides without asking,
   with no `when` that is false in that mode.
3. A `humanGate` with `notify: "auto"` right after the flow's own `user-notification` about the
   same wait — the person gets two messages. Every `gate-notified-twice` warning is one.

# Talking with the person the workflow is for

The person asking for a workflow usually knows their work, not Moira. They can say what they want
done and how they would tell that it went well; they cannot be expected to know what a node, a
condition, a schema or a repair loop is. Hold the requirements conversation in their terms and keep
the engine's terms for the files you write.

## Ask about the goal and about success

Ask what the workflow is for, who runs it, what it produces, and how the person will tell that a
run went well: what they would look at, and what would make them say it failed. Their answers are
the requirements. Turn them into steps, completion conditions and routes yourself.

Do not ask them to design the process ("how many steps", "which conditions", "should this loop").
When a real decision is theirs, ask it as a question about their work: "if the check finds a
problem, should the agent fix it and check again, or stop and tell you?"

## Explain every question and argue your recommendation

Whenever you ask the person something or propose something, explain the options in their terms —
what each means and what follows from it — and give the reasons for your recommendation. They
decide, but they decide knowing why.

## Offer the options with their cost

The same task can be served by a simpler or a more thorough process, and the person should choose
knowing what each costs. Say it in plain words:

- **Simpler** is faster to build and shorter to run. The agent does the steps in order and checks
  the result once at the end.
- **More thorough** takes longer to build and gives a bigger process — designed separately,
  reviewed independently, with checks and redo loops where they matter — and the quality of the
  result is higher.
- **A process can always be improved later.** Starting simple is not a trap: the same workflow can
  be taken through the full design and review path whenever the person wants it.

Recommend the level the task needs rather than the biggest one. The levels are:

- **simple** — steps in order, possibly one choice or one approval; no review-and-redo loop, no
  effect outside the person's own work, no sub-process, no progress view with several stages.
- **standard** — real branches, a review-and-redo loop, approvals, durable files or notes, or
  effects that need the person's authority.
- **complex** — several interacting loops, jumps between parts, sub-processes, locks, a
  multi-stage progress view, publication or other high-authority effects; or any workflow the
  person wants taken through the full path.

## Recommend a starting shape when one fits

Three starting shapes cover most first workflows. Each is a valid workflow in
`reference/templates/`; when one fits, say what it would look like for this task and build from it.

- **Checklist** (`checklist.json`) — steps done in order. Good for onboarding a teammate, a release
  checklist, a daily routine.
- **Do, check, redo** (`do-check-redo.json`) — the work is checked and redone until it passes. This
  is a review-and-redo loop, so it is standard level, not simple.
- **Approval gate** (`approval-gate.json`) — something is prepared, the person approves or declines
  it, and the workflow acts only on approval.

## Agree the level

In an interactive run, propose the level in plain words, with the reason and its cost, and let the
person confirm or change it. In an autonomous run, decide it yourself and write down why, so the
final report can say it.

When the request already says how thorough it should be — "just a quick checklist", "make it more
thorough", "take it through the full path" — take the level from that and do not ask again.

workflow_template_approval_gate.description: Starting template: prepare, ask for approval, act only on approval (simple level); a valid workflow

complexity_tier.description: The level the workflow is authored at: simple, standard or complex. The requirements owner sets it with the person; reviews may only raise it. It decides which authoring responsibilities run and which catalogue sections apply, and is recorded on the workflow as a complexity:<level> tag. Until a requirements owner sets it, the full path applies.

escalation_reason.description: Why a review raised the complexity level during this run, in plain words; empty until a review raises it. Design and the final report read it.

light_repair_pending.description: Whether the light review's repair has answered since the light review last answered: the repair sets it to yes, the light review clears it. The light review mentions the repair's answer only while it is yes, so a repair answer from before a rebuild is never taken as current.

planned_changes.description: What the build will produce: the stages of a new workflow or the planned changes of an edit, one short title each, in build order; the plan list people see in notifications and on the run page

planned_done.description: How many planned stages or changes the build has produced: the whole list once the build finishes, none when a plan is announced

workflow_name.description: The name of the created or edited workflow, as its metadata states it; shown to people when the run finishes

workflow_version.description: The version of the created or edited workflow, as its metadata states it; shown to people when the run finishes
